title: The bed of arrows
hookLine: two kinds of arrows reach Bhishma, and he can tell them apart
carry: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred
tomorrow: his head is hanging down. what pillow will he take?

cards: Two kinds of arrows are flying at Bhishma's chariot. Some come from Shikhandi, standing in front, exactly as Bhishma himself advised. Bhishma doesn't answer them.

He keeps his bow lowered toward that one warrior, the way he said he would. And behind Shikhandi, using him as cover, Arjuna is shooting too. Bhishma has trained and fought beside these archers for a lifetime.
Today, the moment he stops guessing whose arrows are reaching him.

teach.b: In Ganguli's English, Bhishma speaks as the arrows pierce him. These aren't Shikhandi's, he says, in effect. They cut too deep.
These are Arjuna's. Still he doesn't turn his weapons on Shikhandi. Then he falls from his chariot.
So many arrows are lodged in him that he never touches the ground. He lies on them, held above the earth, on a bed of arrows. The fighting stops.
Both sides gather around the same old man. And Bhishma doesn't die. Long ago his father gave him a gift for his vow: he would die only when he chose.
Hindus call it ichchha-mrityu, death at will.

Lying there, he sees the sun in its southern course and decides it isn't yet time. Sages come to him as swans, sent by his mother, the river goddess Ganga, and he tells them he'll hold on until the sun turns north.

Hindu tradition treats the sun's northern half of the year, uttarayana, as the bright, auspicious time, and the Bhagavad Gita names those six months among the bright paths by which those who know God depart.

So Bhishma doesn't just pick a day. He picks a holy one. Hindus still keep the memory: Makar Sankranti is celebrated as the sun's turn north, and Bhishma Ashtami, a few weeks later, marks the day tradition says he let go.
The teaching: in Hinduism, the hour of leaving this life isn't something to hide from. It can be faced, prepared for, and offered to God.

how: Many Hindus remember Bhishma around Makar Sankranti and on Bhishma Ashtami, and the bed of arrows, in Sanskrit shara-shayya, appears in temple art, paintings and retellings of the epic.

o: the swans that carry the old warrior's body home to the river
the single arrow from Shikhandi that ends the old man's life
the grandsire brought down, held on arrows until he chooses to die

s: Bhishma fought back hard against Shikhandi at the end
he kept his weapons from Shikhandi, as he had said he would.
when Bhishma fell, his body never touched the ground
the arrows held him up: a bed of arrows.
Bhishma died the moment he fell
his father's gift let him choose his hour, and he chose to wait for the sun to turn north.

games.q: your cousin says the Hindu idea of a good time to die is just superstition. by Bhishma's story, what's closest?
o: given the choice, Bhishma waited for uttarayana, the holy northern course of the sun; the hour of leaving can be offered to God.
Bhishma only waited because he was too stubborn to give up.
timing mattered only for kings and warriors, never for ordinary people.
games.why: Bhishma could die whenever he chose, and he chose the sun's bright, northern half, the time the Gita names among the bright paths.

practice: Turn toward wherever the sun is right now, even through a wall. Many Hindus greet the sun each morning, palms together or pouring out a little water, with a simple line: Om suryaya namah. I bow to the sun.
Breathe in and feel the light on your face, or imagine it. Breathe out and say the line once, silently or aloud. If you pray, let the greeting be your prayer.
If you don't, let the light remind you that your days have a direction.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma's fall. The grandsire on a bed of arrows, held above the ground, waiting for the sun to turn north.

orig.note: bed of arrows: the name for Bhishma's resting place on the field.

carryVoice: Your line: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred. Bhishma chose a holy one. Day eight hundred twenty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Bhishma-vadha Parva), Bhishma's fall, the bed of arrows, the swans and his decision to wait
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Shantanu's gift to Bhishma of choosing the time of his death
Bhagavad Gita 8.24, the six months of the sun's northern course among the bright paths of departure
